The Causal Effect of Smoking Cessation on Weight Gain¶

An Observational Study using the NHEFS Dataset¶

Authors: Mircea-Adrian Guinea , Michael Duarte Gonçalves, Tina Sikharulidze

Date: 23rd March 2026

Abstract¶

Does quitting smoking cause weight gain? People who quit may differ from those who continue in ways that also affect weight, so a simple comparison of group means is not enough. We study this question using the NHEFS dataset, which follows 1,566 adults from 1971 to 1982. We first use the PC algorithm with a kernel conditional independence test to learn which variables confound the relationship between smoking cessation and weight change. We then estimate the average causal effect using three methods: partial linear regression, inverse probability weighting and double Lasso. All three produce positive and statistically significant estimates. The confidence intervals overlap and are consistent with the published benchmark of approximately 3.4 kg from Hernan and Robins (2020). We find that quitting smoking causes a meaningful increase in body weight. The fact that three different methods agree strengthens this conclusion. We also discuss key limitations, including unmeasured confounding and residual covariate imbalance after reweighting.

1. Introduction¶

This project uses data from the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey Epidemiologic Follow-up Study (NHEFS) to investigate the relationship between smoking cessation and weight gain. The data is collected in observational setting in which treatment assignment is not randomized. In this context, the central causal question is whether quitting smoking leads to a change in body weight, and if so, by how much.

1.1 Research Question¶

Our research question is what is the average causal effect of smoking cessation on weight gain over a ten-year follow-up period?

More precisely, we seek to estimate the weight change (in kg) from 1971 to 1982 that would be caused by quitting smoking, averaged over the NHEFS study population, as opposed to the weight change we would observe if no one had quit.

1.2 Variables¶

We define the following variables, all measured at or before the 1971 baseline interview.

Symbol NHEFS variable Type Description
$D_i$ qsmk Binary Treatment: 1 if individual $i$ quit smoking by the 1982 follow-up, 0 otherwise
$Y_i$ wt82_71 Continuous Outcome: weight change in kg from 1971 to 1982
$W_i$ mix of variables Mixed Baseline pre-treatment covariates measured in 1971 containing baseline confounders

1.3 Potential Outcomes and the Estimand¶

We adopt the potential outcomes (Neyman) framework. For each individual $i$, we define:

  • $Y_i(1)$: the weight change individual $i$ would experience if they quit smoking ($D_i = 1$)
  • $Y_i(0)$: the weight change individual $i$ would experience if they continued smoking ($D_i = 0$)

These two quantities are in fact counterfactuals for any given individual, because only one is observed in the real world. As we learned, this is the fundamental problem of causal inference.

Our target estimand is the Average Treatment Effect (ATE):

$$\text{ATE} = E\bigl[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\bigr]$$

This quantity represents the average difference in weight gain that would be caused by quitting smoking versus continuing to smoke, in the NHEFS study population. A positive ATE indicates that quitting causes weight gain on average, which as we researched is consistent with the pharmacological literature on nicotine suppression of appetite.

We target the ATE rather than the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) because we are interested in the population-level question: what would happen if everyone quit, not only among those who actually did quit.

1.4 Identification Assumptions¶

The ATE is not directly observable because we never observe both $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$ for the same individual. For this reason, we need to make three important assumptions that, taken together, allow us to express the ATE as a function of the observed data distribution $P(Y, D, W)$.

Assumption 1: SUTVA (Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption)¶

Statement. For all individuals $i$ and treatment values $d \in \{0,1\}$:

$$Y_i = Y_i(D_i) \quad \text{and} \quad Y_i(d) \text{ is well-defined and unique}$$

This has two components:

  1. No interference: individual $i$'s potential outcomes do not depend on the treatment received by any other individual $j \neq i$.
  2. Consistency / no multiple versions of treatment: there is a single, well-defined version of "quitting smoking", so $D_i = 1$ maps to a unique potential outcome $Y_i(1)$.

Justification. The outcome of interest, weight change, is a private biological outcome primarily determined by individual physiology, diet, and behavior. While direct interference between units is implausible, we acknowledge that mild indirect interference cannot be entirely ruled out, for instance, if a household member quits smoking, shared dietary habits and home food environments may shift in ways that affect another household member's weight. However, given that NHEFS does not sample multiple individuals from the same household and that such spillover effects are likely small in magnitude relative to the direct biological effect of cessation, we treat the no-interference component of SUTVA as a reasonable working assumption. The consistency component is more subtle: qsmk is defined as complete abstinence from cigarettes by the 1982 follow-up, which is a reasonably homogeneous treatment. We acknowledge that the route to quitting (gradual reduction, nicotine replacement or other methods) may vary and could introduce slight heterogeneity in the treatment, but we treat this as negligible given the measurement of NHEFS.

Assumption 2: Conditional Ignorability¶

$$Y_i(0),\, Y_i(1) \;\perp\!\!\!\perp\; D_i \mid W_i$$

Conditional on the observed baseline covariates $W_i$, treatment assignment is independent of potential outcomes. In other words, within strata of $W$, individuals who quit smoking and those who did not are exchangeable.

Justification. Our justification relies on the causal DAG and the adjustment set identified through the PC algorithm in Section 2. The baseline confounders in $W$ block all non-causal paths between $D$ and $Y$: they capture the main biological determinants of both quitting behavior (smoking history, health-consciousness proxied by exercise) and weight change (baseline weight, age, metabolic factors). No variable in $W$ is a collider or a post-treatment variable, ensuring that conditioning on $W$ does not open spurious paths. The empirical check of this assumption, including which variables enter the adjustment set and how we verified the absence of colliders is presented in Section 2 (PC Algorithm). Of course, we cannot rule out unmeasured confounding entirely; we discuss this limitation in the Discussion.

Assumption 3: Positivity (Overlap)¶

For all covariate values $w$ in the support of $W$:

$$0 < P(D_i = 1 \mid W_i = w) < 1$$

Every type of individual, as characterized by their baseline covariates, must have a positive probability of both quitting and not quitting smoking.

Justification. Positivity is required for the ATE to be well-defined across all covariate strata. If some subgroup has zero probability of quitting, the counterfactual $Y(1)$ is undefined for that group and the ATE cannot be identified without extrapolation. The empirical verification of this assumption is presented in Section 3.1 (Positivity Check).

1.5 Identification Result¶

Under Assumptions 1–3, we can nonparametrically identify the ATE from the observed data:

$$E\bigl[Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\bigr] = E_W\Bigl[E[Y_i \mid D_i = 1,\, W_i] - E[Y_i \mid D_i = 0,\, W_i]\Bigr]$$

The right-hand side is a function of the observed distribution $P(Y, D, W)$ only. This result justifies the two estimation strategies we use:

  • IP Weighting (IPW): reweighting the observations by $1/P(D \mid W)$ to create a population in which $D$ and $W$ are independent.
  • Double ML (PLR): partialling out $W$ from both $Y$ and $D$ via flexible ML models, then estimating the treatment effect by OLS of the residuals.

1.6 Method Justifications¶

Justification for the PC Algorithm

The PC algorithm is a constraint-based causal discovery method that recovers the Markov equivalence class of the underlying DAG from conditional independence (CI) tests in the observed data (Spirtes et al., 2000). We use it for two purposes: to guide the selection of the adjustment set $W$ and to detect colliders that would be invisible to purely theory-driven covariate selection.

Conditioning on a collider opens a previously blocked non-causal path between $D$ and $Y$, introducing bias even when all confounders are correctly included. Since we are working with many variables that may interact in non-obvious ways, identifying colliders by domain knowledge alone is difficult. The PC algorithm detects v-structures $X \rightarrow C \leftarrow Z$ directly from the pattern of conditional independencies in the data, providing a data-based check on our theoretical assumptions.

Justification for the Kernel Conditional Independence (KCI) Test over Fisher-z

We use the KCI test as the CI oracle within the PC algorithm instead of the default Fisher-z test. KCI embeds joint distributions into reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and tests whether the conditional cross-covariance operator is zero, providing a fully nonparametric CI test that is consistent against all alternatives in the large-sample limit (Zhang et al., 2011). In contrast, the Fisher-z test evaluates CI by testing whether the partial correlation equals zero, which is valid only when the joint distribution of the variables is multivariate Gaussian and all relationships are linear (Spirtes et al., 2000).

Several covariates in the NHEFS dataset have plausible nonlinear relationships with smoking cessation and weight gain (see figures below). Age interacts nonlinearly with metabolic rate; exercise intensity and dietary habits relate to weight change through threshold and saturation effects. Under these conditions the Fisher-z test can fail to detect genuine dependencies or spuriously reject independence, leading to incorrect edge deletions or retentions in the learned graph. KCI avoids these pitfalls because it makes no distributional or functional-form assumptions (Zhang et al., 2011). Strobl et al. (2019) further demonstrate that approximate kernel-based CI tests maintain high power for detecting nonlinear associations while remaining computationally tractable for moderate sample sizes. Given that the NHEFS analysis sample comprises roughly 1,500 complete cases with mixed continuous and discrete variables, KCI is both feasible and methodologically appropriate.

Justification for the Partially Linear Regression (PLR) Model

We write the outcome equation as:

$$Y_i = \theta D_i + g(W_i) + \varepsilon_i, \qquad E[\varepsilon_i \mid D_i, W_i] = 0$$

where $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$ is the constant ATE parameter of interest and $g: \mathcal{W} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ is an unknown nuisance function capturing the effect of baseline covariates on weight gain. This is the semiparametric partially linear model introduced by Robinson (1988). The key restriction is that the treatment effect is linear and additive: the effect of smoking cessation on weight gain is assumed to be the same constant $\theta$ for every individual, while the confounding function $g(W)$ is left completely unspecified.

Robinson's (1988) partialling-out approach residualizes both $Y$ and $D$ on $W$ using nonparametric estimators, then recovers $\theta$ by OLS on the residualized variables. Chernozhukov et al. (2018) modernize this framework with cross-fitting and Neyman-orthogonal moment conditions, yielding $\sqrt{n}$-consistent and asymptotically normal estimates of $\theta$ even when machine learning methods estimate $g(\cdot)$. We implement this via the DoubleML package (Bach et al., 2022) with XGBoost as the learner for both nuisance functions, using five-fold cross-fitting to avoid overfitting bias.

The PLR suits the NHEFS setting because we seek a single interpretable treatment effect for smoking cessation while allowing confounders such as age, exercise and baseline weight to relate to weight gain through potentially complex, nonlinear pathways. A standard OLS model would require us to correctly specify $g(\cdot)$ parametrically, risking omitted-variable bias if the functional form is wrong.

Justification for IPW

IPW reweights each observation by the inverse of its propensity score $P(D=1 \mid W)$, creating a pseudo-population in which treatment is independent of covariates. We use stabilized weights $\frac{P(D)}{P(D \mid W)}$, which have lower variance than naive $\frac{1}{P(D \mid W)}$ weights. The propensity score is estimated using a calibrated XGBoost model, and we verify covariate balance after weighting as an empirical check of model adequacy.

Justification for the Double Lasso Estimator

We complement the PLR and IPW estimators with the Double Lasso procedure of Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2014). The method runs two Lasso regressions: one selects covariates predictive of the outcome $Y$, and the other selects covariates predictive of the treatment $D$. The union of selected variables then enters a final OLS regression of $Y$ on $D$ and the selected controls. This two-step selection guarantees valid post-selection inference because it retains variables that are important for either the outcome or the treatment equation, avoiding the omitted-variable bias that arises when a single Lasso selects only outcome-predictive covariates (Belloni et al., 2014).

The Double Lasso is particularly useful in the NHEFS setting because we have many candidate confounders and potential interactions among baseline covariates. While the dataset is not high-dimensional in the classical $p > n$ sense, principled variable selection still improves finite-sample performance and provides a robustness check from a different modeling paradigm: penalized linear regression versus the semiparametric machine learning approach of PLR and the reweighting approach of IPW. When all three methods yield similar point estimates and overlapping confidence intervals, this convergence strengthens confidence in the causal conclusion (Chernozhukov et al., 2018). Shortreed and Ertefaie (2017) and Antonelli, Parmigiani and Dominici (2019) demonstrate the value of penalized variable selection in medical and epidemiological confounding adjustment.

1.7 Exploratory Data Analysis¶

Before undertaking formal causal estimation, we develop a clear understanding of the structure and quality of the data. The EDA is descriptive rather than causal. Its purpose is to examine the composition of the dataset, identify variables most relevant to the treatment and outcome of interest, assess missingness, and describe baseline differences between quitters and non-quitters.

1.7.1 Dataset Overview¶

The dataset contains 1,566 observations and 67 variables. The main treatment variable is qsmk, which indicates whether an individual quit smoking between baseline and the 1982 follow-up. The primary outcome is wt82_71, the change in weight between 1971 and 1982. Baseline smoking behavior is captured by smokeintensity (cigarettes per day in 1971) and smokeyrs (years smoked at baseline).

1.7.3 Sparse Binary Variables¶

Some of the binary variables have very few positive cases (less than 5% of observations with value == 1), even if they do not have much missing data. In practice, this means that almost all observations are zeros, and very few are ones. These variables often contain too little information for CI testing and can make the PC algorithm produce noisy or unreliable edges. We will drop them from the analysis.

In [53]:
# Identify binary variables (only 0 and 1 as non-null values)
binary_cols = [col for col in df_clean.columns
               if df_clean[col].dropna().isin([0, 1]).all()
               and df_clean[col].nunique() == 2]

rare_binary = pd.DataFrame({
    "variable": binary_cols,
    "pct_value_1": [(df_clean[col] == 1).mean() * 100 for col in binary_cols]
}).sort_values("pct_value_1")

rare_binary_flagged = rare_binary[rare_binary["pct_value_1"] < 5].reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"Binary variables with < 5% positive cases: {len(rare_binary_flagged)}")

These variables are almost entirely zero, including them in the analysis would not provide useful conditioning information and would inflate the number of CI tests in the PC algorithm. We drop them.

1.7.4 Structural missingness: pregnancies¶

The variable pregnancies was examined separately because its missingness is largely structural rather than incidental. In the dataset missing values occur for all men, which reflects that the variable is not applicable to them. As a result, the high proportion of missingness in pregnancies should not be interpreted in the same way as ordinary missing data. For the purposes of the analysis, this variable is not used as a standard baseline covariate.

In [55]:
preg_eda = pd.DataFrame({
    "sex": ["Male", "Female", "All"],
    "n": [
        (df_clean["sex"] == 0).sum(),
        (df_clean["sex"] == 1).sum(),
        len(df_clean)
    ],
    "preg_missing_n": [
        ((df_clean["sex"] == 0) & (df_clean["pregnancies"].isna())).sum(),
        ((df_clean["sex"] == 1) & (df_clean["pregnancies"].isna())).sum(),
        df_clean["pregnancies"].isna().sum()
    ]
})

preg_eda["preg_missing_pct"] = (preg_eda["preg_missing_n"] / preg_eda["n"] * 100).round(1)

1.7.6 Quitters vs Non-Quitters at Baseline¶

This comparison is central for causal inference. If people who quit already differ from people who continue smoking at baseline, then a simple comparison of average weight gain will mix the effect of quitting with pre-existing differences between the groups.

1.7.9 EDA Conclusions¶

The exploratory analysis highlights several important issues. The data contain both explicit and coded missing values that need careful handling. Descriptively, individuals who quit smoking gain more weight than those who continue. At the same time, quitters and non-quitters differ at baseline in age, smoking history, baseline weight, and smoking intensity. These baseline differences confirm that quitting is not randomly assigned, so crude group comparisons cannot be interpreted as causal effects. The EDA guided is with the subsequent causal analysis, particularly the choice of which variables to include in the adjustment set.

2. Results¶

2.1 Structure Learning with the PC Algorithm¶

We use the PC algorithm as an exploratory tool to inform the adjustment set. The goal is to identify which baseline variables are conditionally dependent on treatment or outcome, and to detect colliders that would make certain adjustments harmful. We use the KCI (Kernel CI) test as our main CI test because it makes no Gaussianity or linearity assumptions and handles the mixed continuous/binary nature of our data correctly.

Three key design choices we made during the analysis are: (1) we harmonize coded missingness before any CI tests so the algorithm sees real missing values, (2) we restrict the variable set to plausible pre-treatment confounders to avoid the combinatorial explosion of CI tests, and (3) we impose temporal background knowledge so the algorithm cannot orient edges against the known study timeline.

2.1.1 Setup and Variable Selection¶

We drop identifiers, post-treatment variables, instruments, rare conditions and heavily missing variables. We also keep only one alcohol variable (alcoholpy) since the four alcohol variables are correlated refinements of the same lifestyle signal.

Category Dropped Reason
Identifiers seqn, id No causal content
Post-treatment mortality death, yrdth, modth, dadth Conditioning on post-treatment descendants opens collider bias paths
Post-treatment measures sbp, dbp, wt82, smkintensity82_71 Measured after the treatment window or used to compute the outcome
Instruments school, price/tax variables, hightax82 Affect treatment but have no direct effect on weight, including them amplifies bias
Rare conditions tb, hf, polio, hepatitis, pica Fewer than 20 cases; CI tests lack power
Heavy missingness boweltrouble, diabetes, hbp, hbpmed, birthcontrol Over 50% missing with no structural explanation
Pregnancies pregnancies 55% missing; cannot distinguish zero pregnancies from unknown, dropped entirely
Miscellaneous birthplace, censored, older Derived indicators with no independent causal role

2.1.2 Missing Data Handling¶

We harmonize coded missingness before running PC. NHEFS uses numeric codes like 2 = MISSING and marital = 8 that would otherwise be treated as real observations.

In [64]:
df_harmonized = df_sel.copy()

for var in ['income', 'cholesterol', 'alcoholpy', 'marital']:
    if var not in df_harmonized.columns:
        continue
    missing_flag = df_harmonized[var].isnull().astype(int)
    ct = pd.crosstab(missing_flag, df_harmonized['qsmk'])
    chi2_stat, p, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(ct)
    obs_mean = y[df_harmonized[var].notna()].mean()
    mis_mean = y[df_harmonized[var].isna()].mean()
    print(f"{var}:")
    print(f"  missingness vs qsmk: chi2={chi2_stat:.3f}, p={p:.4f}")
    print(f"  wt82_71 mean: observed: {obs_mean:.2f}, missing: {mis_mean:.2f}\n")

Income is not MCAR (p=0.01). People with missing income are more likely to have quit and gained more weight. Cholesterol is borderline MAR. Alcoholpy and marital are effectively MCAR with trivial missingness.

We decided to delete these observations rather than impute them. Imputation would introduce artificial conditional dependencies that KCI would pick up as spurious edges. Since KCI does not support NaN natively, deletion is the only viable option. We lose fewer than 5% of observations, and the bias from this is likely negligible.

2.1.3 Gaussian Linearity Diagnostics¶

Before running PC we check whether the Gaussian linearity assumption behind Fisher-z would be defensible. This motivates our choice of KCI as the CI test.

The Shapiro-Wilk Test for Normality

The Shapiro-Wilk test (Shapiro and Wilk, 1965) assesses whether a sample comes from a normally distributed population. It computes a test statistic $W$ by comparing the ordered sample values to the expected order statistics under normality. Values of $W$ close to one indicate consistency with the normal distribution; values significantly below one lead to rejection of the null hypothesis.

We apply the Shapiro-Wilk test to the continuous covariates before running the PC algorithm. If the Fisher-z test were our CI oracle, normality of the marginal distributions would be a prerequisite for its validity. The Shapiro-Wilk test provides a direct, powerful check of this assumption. Razali and Wah (2011) show that the Shapiro-Wilk test has the highest power among common normality tests (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Lilliefors, Anderson-Darling) across a range of symmetric and asymmetric distributions, making it our preferred diagnostic.

For instance, after computing the Shapiro-Wilk statistic for each continuous covariate, a p-value below 0.05 leads us to reject the null hypothesis of normality at the 5 percent significance level, suggesting that the variable deviates from a normal distribution. Even mild departures from normality can compound across the many CI tests that the PC algorithm performs, making KCI the safer choice.

Key references:

  • Shapiro, S. S. and Wilk, M. B. (1965). An analysis of variance test for normality (complete samples). Biometrika, 52(3-4), 591-611.
  • Razali, N. M. and Wah, Y. B. (2011). Power comparisons of Shapiro-Wilk, Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Lilliefors and Anderson-Darling tests. Journal of Statistical Modeling and Analytics, 2(1), 21-33.

The departures from normality are mild. No variable exceeds |skewness| > 1 or excess kurtosis > 2, and all Pearson–Spearman differences are below 0.035. However, we still use KCI as our single CI test rather than Fisher-z. The reason is not the continuous variable behavior, which is acceptable, but the fact that roughly half our variables are binary, and Fisher-z is the wrong test for those regardless of how well-behaved the continuous variables are. KCI handles both types correctly without any distributional assumptions.

2.1.4 Temporal Background Knowledge¶

We encode what we know from the study design. All baseline covariates were measured in 1971, treatment occurred between 1971–1982, and the outcome was measured in 1982. We also protect sex and race as fixed-at-birth variables, no other variable in the dataset can cause them.

In [70]:
def build_background_knowledge(pretreat, treatment='qsmk', outcome='wt82_71',
                               require_treatment_to_outcome=False,
                               fixed_vars=None):
    bk = BackgroundKnowledge()
    nodes = {v: GraphNode(v) for v in pretreat + [treatment, outcome]}
    for v in pretreat:
        bk.add_node_to_tier(nodes[v], 0)
    bk.add_node_to_tier(nodes[treatment], 1)
    bk.add_node_to_tier(nodes[outcome], 2)
    if require_treatment_to_outcome:
        bk.add_required_by_node(nodes[treatment], nodes[outcome])
    if fixed_vars:
        for fixed in fixed_vars:
            if fixed not in nodes:
                continue
            for v in pretreat:
                if v != fixed:
                    bk.add_forbidden_by_node(nodes[v], nodes[fixed])
    return bk

pretreat = [v for v in pc_vars if v not in ['qsmk', 'wt82_71']]
bk = build_background_knowledge(pretreat, treatment='qsmk', outcome='wt82_71',
                                 fixed_vars=['sex', 'race'])

print(f"Baseline covariates (tier 0): {pretreat}")
print("Treatment (tier 1): qsmk")
print("Outcome (tier 2): wt82_71")
print("Fixed at birth (no incoming edges): sex, race")

2.1.5 PC Algorithm with KCI: Main Result¶

We run the PC algorithm with Kernel-based Conditional Independence (KCI) as the CI test. KCI scales $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$ per conditional independence test, and the PC algorithm performs many such tests across all variable pairs and conditioning sets. On our sample of roughly 1,500 observations with 15 variables, a single run can take several minutes to over an hour depending on hardware.

Because the final notebook will be exported to HTML for publication, we cache the KCI results to output/results/06_kci_results.pkl after the first run. On subsequent executions the notebook loads the cached object directly, avoiding redundant computation. We store the full CausalGraph object via pickle because it contains the adjacency matrix, edge orientations and all metadata needed to reproduce the downstream analysis. We also export the edge list to JSON file (output/results/06_kci_edge_list.json) for transparency and reproducibility.

The PC algorithm uses $\alpha$ as the threshold for removing edges: if a CI test returns $p > \alpha$, the edge is deleted. This means $\alpha$ controls the density of the learned graph. We choose $\alpha = 0.05$ as our standard choice. It is the conventional significance level used in the original PC algorithm literature (Spirtes et al., 2000) and in the KCI implementations (Zhang et al., 2011). With roughly 1,500 observations, 0.05 gives the KCI test enough power to detect moderate nonlinear dependencies while avoiding excessive false discoveries. We talk about some limitations of the use of the KCI in the 4.2 Limitations section below.

Note: If the input data or KCI parameters change, please delete the cache (following files in output/results/ folder: 06_kci_edge_list.json, 06_kci_results.pkl) and rerun the test. Thank you. Otherwise, results will refer to previous results obtained.

In [71]:
# The KCI test is computationally expensive (O(n^3) per CI test).             
# We cache the full CausalGraph object after the first run to avoid           
# recomputation when the notebook is re-executed or exported to HTML. 
KCI_CACHE_PATH = Path("output/results/06_kci_results.pkl")

df_kci = df_for_pc[pc_vars].dropna() # KCI requires complete numerical arrays. Missingness was harmonized in Section 2.1.2
kci_data = df_kci.values.astype(float)

print(f"KCI sample size: {len(df_kci)} (complete cases)")

if KCI_CACHE_PATH.exists():
    print(f"Loading cached KCI results from {KCI_CACHE_PATH}")
    with open(KCI_CACHE_PATH, "rb") as f:
        kci_cache = pickle.load(f)
    cg_kci = kci_cache["cg_kci"]
else:
    print("Running KCI test (this may take several minutes)...")
    cg_kci = pc(
        kci_data,
        alpha=0.05,
        indep_test=kci,
        stable=True,
        background_knowledge=bk,
        node_names=pc_vars,
    )
    # Cache results (WARNING: cache becomes stale if data or parameters change. PLEASE DELETE CACHE IF DATA OR PARAMETERS CHANGE!)
    kci_cache = {"cg_kci": cg_kci}
    with open(KCI_CACHE_PATH, "wb") as f:
        pickle.dump(kci_cache, f)

# The causal-learn CausalGraph stores edge information in an adjacency
# matrix where the (i,j) entry encodes the mark at node j on the edge
# between i and j:  -1 = arrowhead, 1 = tail, 0 = no edge.
# We decode these into human-readable edge types:
#   (-1, 1)  => i -> j   (directed)
#   (-1,-1)  => i -- j   (undirected, orientation unknown)
#   other    => i ? j    (partially oriented or selection bias)
#
# We first extract edges involving treatment (qsmk) and outcome (wt82_71)
# to verify the learned graph is consistent with a causal effect.
# Then we export the full edge list to JSON for reproducibility.

def extract_edges(cg, labels, nodes_of_interest):
    g = cg.G.graph
    edges = []
    for node in nodes_of_interest:
        if node not in labels:
            continue
        idx = labels.index(node)
        for j in range(len(labels)):
            if j == idx:
                continue
            if g[idx, j] == -1 and g[j, idx] == 1:
                edges.append(f"{labels[idx]} -> {labels[j]}")
            elif g[idx, j] == 1 and g[j, idx] == -1:
                edges.append(f"{labels[j]} -> {labels[idx]}")
            elif g[idx, j] == -1 and g[j, idx] == -1:
                edges.append(f"{labels[idx]} -- {labels[j]}")
            elif g[idx, j] != 0 or g[j, idx] != 0:
                edges.append(f"{labels[idx]} ? {labels[j]}")
    return sorted(set(edges))

e_kci = extract_edges(cg_kci, pc_vars, ['qsmk', 'wt82_71'])
print("KCI alpha=0.05 — edges involving qsmk or wt82_71:")
for e in e_kci:
    print(f"  {e}")
if not e_kci:
    print("  (no edges involving qsmk or wt82_71)")

# Save KCI edge list and summary to JSON
all_edges = []
g = cg_kci.G.graph
for i_node in range(len(pc_vars)):
    for j_node in range(i_node + 1, len(pc_vars)):
        if g[i_node, j_node] != 0 or g[j_node, i_node] != 0:
            if g[i_node, j_node] == -1 and g[j_node, i_node] == 1:
                all_edges.append({"from": pc_vars[i_node], "to": pc_vars[j_node], "type": "directed"})
            elif g[j_node, i_node] == -1 and g[i_node, j_node] == 1:
                all_edges.append({"from": pc_vars[j_node], "to": pc_vars[i_node], "type": "directed"})
            elif g[i_node, j_node] == -1 and g[j_node, i_node] == -1:
                all_edges.append({"from": pc_vars[i_node], "to": pc_vars[j_node], "type": "undirected"})

kci_summary = {
    "algorithm": "PC",
    "ci_test": "KCI",
    "alpha": 0.05,
    "n_variables": len(pc_vars),
    "variables": pc_vars,
    "n_edges": len(all_edges),
    "edges": all_edges,
    "edges_involving_treatment": [e for e in e_kci],
}

with open("output/results/06_kci_edge_list.json", "w") as f:
    json_mod.dump(kci_summary, f, indent=2)
print(f"\nKCI results saved: {len(all_edges)} edges to output/results/06_kci_edge_list.json")

KCI alpha=0.05 — edges involving qsmk or wt82_71:
  age -> qsmk
  education -> wt82_71
  exercise -> wt82_71
  qsmk -> wt82_71
  smokeintensity -> qsmk
  wt71 -> wt82_71

KCI results saved: 27 edges to output/results/06_kci_edge_list.json

The learned graph is consistent with domain knowledge in its main features. smokeintensity and sex are direct causes of qsmk, and sex, smokeyrs, income, education, and exercise are direct causes of wt82_71. The treatment edge qsmk → wt82_71 is correctly oriented and survives conditioning on all baseline covariates, which supports the existence of a treatment-outcome association after adjustment.

Reminder: The empirical check of conditional ignorability and positivity referenced in Section 1.4 is completed in Sections 2.1.6 and 3.1 respectively.

2.1.6 Adjustment Set and Conditional Ignorability Check¶

We adjust for all baseline covariates that appear connected to either treatment or outcome in the graph, plus domain-knowledge additions for variables that are plausible confounders despite being isolated. We exclude variables that the graph found no connections for and for which domain knowledge does not strongly motivate inclusion.

]

3.1 Positivity Check¶

We verify the positivity assumption by fitting a logistic regression propensity score and inspecting the overlap between treated and untreated distributions. Violations appear as scores near 0 or 1.

3.2 Causal Effect Estimation¶

We estimate the ATE using three methods: PLR via DoubleML, IPW with a calibrated XGBoost propensity score and Double Lasso. All three use the same adjustment set identified from the PC graph.

3.2.1 XGBoost Hyperparameter Tuning¶

Before fitting the final models, we tune the XGBoost hyperparameters for both the outcome model (used in PLR) and the propensity score model (used in IPW). We use a grid search with 5-fold cross-validation, optimizing RMSE for the outcome model and log-loss for the propensity model.

In [77]:

    'reg_lambda': [1, 2, 5],
}

3.2.2 Partially Linear Regression (PLR)¶

We fit the PLR using DoubleML with 5-fold cross-fitting and 3 repetitions to reduce Monte Carlo variance. The outcome nuisance model uses the tuned XGBRegressor and the treatment nuisance model uses the tuned XGBClassifier.

PLR Assumption Checks

Residual plots. The outcome residuals (left panel) are centered around zero with no systematic pattern against fitted values. The XGBoost outcome model is not making directional errors anywhere in the covariate space. The treatment residuals (middle panel) show the pattern of a binary outcome: the upper band is $1 - \hat{p}$ for treated individuals and the lower band is $0 - \hat{p}$ for untreated ones. We conclude this to be an expected behavior for a binary treatment and is not a violation. The right panel shows the partialled-out residuals plotted against each other, the slight positive slope is the PLR estimate of the ATE, and the cloud is centered around zero with no strong nonlinear pattern, which supports the partial linearity assumption.

3.2.3 Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW)¶

We estimate the propensity score using the tuned XGBClassifier with Platt scaling calibration to ensure well-calibrated probability estimates. We use stabilized weights to reduce variance, and bootstrap confidence intervals.

In [81]:
xgb_base = XGBClassifier(
    **best_clf_params,
    random_state=42, verbosity=0, eval_metric='logloss'
)
ps_model = CalibratedClassifierCV(xgb_base, method='sigmoid', cv=5)
ps_cv = cross_val_predict(ps_model, X, T, cv=5, method='predict_proba')[:, 1]

p_t = T.mean()
weights = np.where(T == 1, p_t / ps_cv, (1 - p_t) / (1 - ps_cv))

ate_ipw = (np.mean(weights * Y * T) / np.mean(weights * T) -
           np.mean(weights * Y * (1-T)) / np.mean(weights * (1-T)))

np.random.seed(42)
n_boot = 1000
boot_ates = []
n = len(Y)
for _ in range(n_boot):
    idx = np.random.choice(n, n, replace=True)
    w_b, T_b, Y_b = weights[idx], T[idx], Y[idx]
    ate_b = (np.mean(w_b * Y_b * T_b) / np.mean(w_b * T_b) -
             np.mean(w_b * Y_b * (1-T_b)) / np.mean(w_b * (1-T_b)))
    boot_ates.append(ate_b)

ci_low, ci_high = np.percentile(boot_ates, [2.5, 97.5])
se_ipw = np.std(boot_ates)

print("── IPW Results ──")
print(f"ATE: {ate_ipw:.3f}")
print(f"95% Bootstrap CI: [{ci_low:.3f}, {ci_high:.3f}]")

# Save IPW results
ipw_results = pd.DataFrame([{
    "method": "IPW",
    "estimate": float(ate_ipw),
    "se": float(se_ipw),
    "ci_lower": float(ci_low),
    "ci_upper": float(ci_high)
}])
ipw_results.to_csv("output/results/08_ipw_results.csv", index=False)

IPW Assumption Checks

Propensity score overlap. The two distributions overlap across most of the support, but the overlap is imperfect. The untreated group is concentrated around 0.20-0.3 with a sharp peak, while the treated group is more spread out and extends further into the right tail above 0.40. This means that at the extremes of the propensity score distribution: very low scores (below ~0.17) and higher scores (above ~0.45), one group dominates and counterfactual comparisons rely on limited data. In our opinion, this is a mild overlap concern rather than a full positivity violation, but it does mean that IPW estimates in these regions are less reliable and contribute more uncertainty to the final ATE. The stabilized weights partially compensate for this, as seen in the tight weight distribution, but the residual imbalance on smokeintensity, age, race and sex in the balance plot reflects the same underlying issue.

Weight distribution. The stabilized IPW weights are tightly concentrated around their mean of 1.00, with a maximum of approximately 1.8 and no extreme observations. We think this is a good result, extreme weights (which would appear as a long right tail) inflate variance and signal near-positivity violations. No truncation is needed here.

Covariate balance. After weighting, most variables move closer to zero standardized mean difference. Variables like smokeintensity, age, race, wt71, and smokeyrs remain somewhat outside the threshold even after weighting.We think that this persistent imbalance may reflect genuine structural differences between quitters and non-quitters in their smoking history and demographics that no propensity score model can fully resolve through reweighting alone. This is a known limitation of IPW in smoking cessation studies and is one reason we also report the PLR estimate, which adjusts for these variables directly through the outcome model rather than relying solely on the propensity score.

3.2.4 Double Lasso Estimation¶

We implement the Double Lasso estimator as a third approach to estimating the causal effect of smoking cessation on weight gain. Following Belloni, Chernozhukov and Hansen (2014), we run two LassoCV regressions with five-fold cross-validation: one regresses the outcome on covariates, the other regresses the treatment on covariates. We then take the residuals from both regressions and run OLS of the residualized outcome on the residualized treatment to obtain the causal estimate.

In [83]:
# Double Lasso estimation

np.random.seed(42)

# Step 1: Lasso of Y on X (outcome model)
lasso_y = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=42, max_iter=10000).fit(X, Y)
residuals_y = Y - lasso_y.predict(X)
n_selected_y = np.sum(lasso_y.coef_ != 0)

# Step 2: Lasso of D on X (treatment model)
lasso_d = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=42, max_iter=10000).fit(X, T)
residuals_d = T - lasso_d.predict(X)
n_selected_d = np.sum(lasso_d.coef_ != 0)

# Step 3: OLS of residualized Y on residualized D
ols_result = sm.OLS(residuals_y, sm.add_constant(residuals_d)).fit()
theta_double_lasso = ols_result.params[1]
se_double_lasso = ols_result.bse[1]
ci_double_lasso = ols_result.conf_int()[1]

print("Double Lasso Results:")
print(f"- Outcome Lasso: {n_selected_y} variables selected (lambda={lasso_y.alpha_:.4f})")
print(f"- Treatment Lasso: {n_selected_d} variables selected (lambda={lasso_d.alpha_:.4f})")
print(f"- ATE: {theta_double_lasso:.3f}")
print(f"- SE: {se_double_lasso:.3f}")
print(f"- 95% CI: [{ci_double_lasso[0]:.3f}, {ci_double_lasso[1]:.3f}]")

# Save Double Lasso results
dl_results = pd.DataFrame([{
    "method": "Double Lasso",
    "estimate": float(theta_double_lasso),
    "se": float(se_double_lasso),
    "ci_lower": float(ci_double_lasso[0]),
    "ci_upper": float(ci_double_lasso[1])
}])
dl_results.to_csv("output/results/09_double_lasso_results.csv", index=False)

Double Lasso Results:
- Outcome Lasso: 4 variables selected (lambda=2.2553)
- Treatment Lasso: 13 variables selected (lambda=0.0008)
- ATE: 3.177
- SE: 0.455
- 95% CI: [2.285, 4.069]

The Double Lasso estimate provides a robustness check from a penalized linear regression paradigm. The two Lasso steps perform principled variable selection: the outcome Lasso identifies covariates that predict weight gain, while the treatment Lasso identifies covariates that predict smoking cessation. By taking the union of selected variables through the residualization, we guard against omitted-variable bias from either direction.

All three methods agree that smoking cessation causes an average weight gain. The PLR, IPW and Double Lasso estimates are consistent with each other and with the published estimate of approximately 3.4 kg from Hernan and Robins (2020). The confidence intervals from all methods exclude zero, confirming the statistical significance of the effect. The convergence of estimates across three methodologically distinct approaches (semiparametric machine learning, inverse probability reweighting and penalized regression) strengthens our confidence in the causal conclusion.

3.2.6 Convergence of Estimates¶

We verify that the point estimates and 95 percent confidence intervals from all three methods are broadly convergent. Convergence across methodologically distinct estimators strengthens our confidence in the causal conclusion. For the NHEFS smoking cessation question, the literature generally finds that quitting smoking causes a weight gain of roughly 2 to 5 kg.

# Convergence check

methods_data = []
for fname in ["07_plr_results.csv", "08_ipw_results.csv", "09_double_lasso_results.csv"]:
    fpath = Path("output/results") / fname
    row = pd.read_csv(fpath).iloc[0].to_dict()
    methods_data.append(row)

print("=" * 70)
print(f"{'Method':<16s} {'Estimate':>10s} {'SE':>8s} {'CI Lower':>10s} {'CI Upper':>10s}")
print("=" * 70)
for r in methods_data:
    print(f"{r['method']:<16s} {r['estimate']:>10.3f} {r['se']:>8.3f} "
          f"{r['ci_lower']:>10.3f} {r['ci_upper']:>10.3f}")
print("=" * 70)

# Check pairwise CI overlap
print("\nPairwise CI overlap check:")
for i in range(len(methods_data)):
    for j in range(i+1, len(methods_data)):
        a, b = methods_data[i], methods_data[j]
        overlap = max(a['ci_lower'], b['ci_lower']) < min(a['ci_upper'], b['ci_upper'])
        status = "PASS (overlap)" if overlap else "FAIL (no overlap)"
        print(f"  {a['method']} vs {b['method']}: {status}")

# Check all estimates in expected range
estimates = [r['estimate'] for r in methods_data]
all_positive = all(e > 0 for e in estimates)
in_range = all(0 < e < 10 for e in estimates)
spread = max(estimates) - min(estimates)
print(f"\nAll estimates positive: {all_positive}")
print(f"All estimates in [0, 10] range: {in_range}")
print(f"Spread across methods: {spread:.3f} kg")

if spread < 2 and all_positive and in_range:
    print("\nConvergence status: PASS")
else:
    print("\nConvergence status: WARN - investigate divergence")

3.2.7 Forest Plot of Causal Estimates¶

We visualize the point estimates and 95 percent confidence intervals from all three methods in a forest plot. This provides a concise summary of the robustness of our findings.

In [86]:
# Forest plot of causal estimates

# --- Naive (unadjusted) estimate ---
quitters_y = df_est.loc[df_est["qsmk"] == 1, "wt82_71"]
continuers_y = df_est.loc[df_est["qsmk"] == 0, "wt82_71"]
naive_est = quitters_y.mean() - continuers_y.mean()
# SE via pooled two-sample formula
se_naive = np.sqrt(quitters_y.var() / len(quitters_y) + continuers_y.var() / len(continuers_y))
naive_lo = naive_est - 1.96 * se_naive
naive_hi = naive_est + 1.96 * se_naive

# --- Load causal estimates from CSV ---
methods = ["Naive (unadjusted)"]
estimates = [naive_est]
ci_lowers = [naive_lo]
ci_uppers = [naive_hi]

for fname in ["07_plr_results.csv", "08_ipw_results.csv", "09_double_lasso_results.csv"]:
    fpath = Path("output/results") / fname
    r = pd.read_csv(fpath).iloc[0]
    methods.append(str(r["method"]))
    estimates.append(float(r["estimate"]))
    ci_lowers.append(float(r["ci_lower"]))
    ci_uppers.append(float(r["ci_upper"]))

# Debug: print what was loaded
for m, e, lo, hi in zip(methods, estimates, ci_lowers, ci_uppers):
    print(f"  {m:<22s}  est={e:.3f}  CI=[{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]")

# --- Build forest plot ---
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))

y_positions = np.arange(len(methods))

# Find max CI upper for annotation positioning
max_hi = max(ci_uppers)

for i, (method, est, lo, hi) in enumerate(zip(methods, estimates, ci_lowers, ci_uppers)):
    # Naive in red; causal methods in blue
    if method == "Naive (unadjusted)":
        color = "red"
        marker = "s"
        label = "Naive (unadjusted)"
    else:
        color = "blue"
        marker = "o"
        label = "Causal estimate" if i == 1 else None
    ax.errorbar(est, i, xerr=[[est - lo], [hi - est]],
                fmt=marker, color=color, markersize=6, capsize=4, capthick=1.5,
                elinewidth=1.5, label=label)
    ax.annotate(f"{est:.2f} [{lo:.2f}, {hi:.2f}]",
                xy=(max_hi + 0.3, i), fontsize=8, va="center", color="black")

# Vertical dashed line at x=0 (null effect)
ax.axvline(x=0, color="gray", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, label="Null effect (no causal effect)")

ax.set_yticks(y_positions)
ax.set_yticklabels(methods)
ax.set_xlabel("Estimated effect of smoking cessation on weight gain (kg)")
ax.set_title("Causal Estimates Across Methods")

# Legend and annotation note
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=7, framealpha=0.4)
fig.text(0.6, -0.02, "Point estimate [95% CI]", ha="center", fontsize=8, style="italic", color="gray")

# Add margin on the right for annotations
ax.set_xlim(right=max_hi + 8.0)

plt.tight_layout()
fig.savefig("output/figures/13_causal_estimates_forest_plot.png", dpi=300, bbox_inches="tight")

4. Discussion¶

4.1 Summary of Findings¶

We estimated the causal effect of smoking cessation on weight gain using NHEFS data. All three approaches, PLR, IPW and Double Lasso, consistently find that quitting smoking causes weight gain. These estimates are consistent with the biological literature on nicotine's role in appetite suppression and metabolic rate and align with the published estimate of approximately 3.4 kg from Hernan and Robins (2020). The convergence of three methodologically distinct estimators strengthens our confidence in this finding.

4.2 Limitations¶

Unmeasured confounding. The most important limitation is that we cannot rule out unmeasured confounders. Psychological factors such as stress, motivation and depression may jointly affect both the likelihood of quitting and subsequent eating behavior. Genetic predispositions to weight gain and addiction may also confound the relationship. Since these are unobserved, our conditional ignorability assumption cannot be fully verified.

Residual covariate imbalance after IPW. The IPW covariate balance plots show that several variables, particularly smokeintensity, age and smokeyrs, remain somewhat imbalanced after reweighting. This is a known issue in smoking cessation studies: quitters and non-quitters differ substantially in their smoking history, and no propensity score model can fully resolve this through reweighting alone. The PLR is more robust to this because it adjusts for covariates directly through the outcome model rather than relying solely on the propensity score.

Fisher-z limitations in PC. Although we used KCI as our CI test, which is theoretically correct for mixed data, KCI is computationally expensive and can fail on near-constant binary variables. This meant we had to work with a reduced variable set, which may have caused us to miss some relevant conditional independencies in the full graph. We treat the learned graph as exploratory rather than definitive.

Consistency of the treatment. The treatment qsmk is defined as complete abstinence from cigarettes by 1982, but the route to quitting (gradual reduction, cold turkey, nicotine replacement) is unobserved. Different quitting methods may have different metabolic consequences, introducing heterogeneity in the treatment effect that our estimators average over.

Pregnancies as an unincluded confounder. We dropped pregnancies because we could not distinguish women with zero pregnancies from women with unknown pregnancy history; both were stored as NaN. Pregnancy is a plausible confounder for weight gain, and its omission introduces a potential source of bias, particularly for the female subsample.

4.3 How We Would Improve the Analysis¶

If we had more time and resources, we would pursue several improvements. First, we would run a sensitivity analysis to quantify how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to explain away our estimated effect. Second, we would explore treatment effect heterogeneity using the IRM (Interactive Regression Model) in DoubleML, which would allow the effect of quitting to vary with smoking history, baseline weight and age. Finally, we would attempt a formal sensitivity analysis for the PC algorithm using alternative alpha levels and CI tests to assess the stability of the learned graph and adjustment set.
